flashcards.question: What is MANAGEMENT, and what are the four management FUNCTIONS?
flashcards.answer:
Management = working with human, financial, physical and informational resources to achieve organizational objectives by performing the four functions.

The FOUR FUNCTIONS are:
1. PLANNING — setting objectives and deciding in advance how to meet them
2. ORGANIZING — delegating and coordinating tasks and allocating resources
3. LEADING — influencing employees to work toward objectives
4. CONTROLLING — monitoring progress and taking corrective action
flashcards.explanation: The word derives from Latin 'manus' (hand) + 'agere' (to act). The functions are distinct yet interrelated — performed simultaneously, not as linear steps.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between EFFICIENT and EFFECTIVE?
flashcards.answer:
• EFFICIENT = doing things RIGHT, so as to maximize the utilization of resources (do it with least waste).
• EFFECTIVE = doing the RIGHT thing in order to attain an objective.

High performance = selecting the right resources (effective) AND using them well (efficient).
flashcards.explanation: A manager achieves objectives through efficient AND effective use of resources.

flashcards.question: What are the FOUR organizational RESOURCES managers manage?
flashcards.answer:
1. HUMAN resources — people ('human capital'), the most valuable asset
2. FINANCIAL resources — money/budget needed to operate
3. PHYSICAL resources — products, equipment, materials, supplies
4. INFORMATIONAL resources — information/knowledge to set objectives and make decisions
flashcards.explanation: Performance depends on how well managers acquire and use these four resources.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE management SKILLS?
flashcards.answer:
1. TECHNICAL skills ('hard skills') — ability to use methods/techniques to perform a task; more important for non-managers.
2. INTERPERSONAL skills ('people/soft skills') — ability to understand, communicate and work well with others; increasingly the most important.
3. DECISION-MAKING skills — ability to conceptualize situations and select alternatives to solve problems / seize opportunities.
flashcards.explanation: Technical skills matter more at lower levels; decision-making skills matter more at the top (e.g. Reed Hastings at Netflix).

flashcards.question: What are Mintzberg's 10 MANAGEMENT ROLES, grouped into 3 categories?
flashcards.answer:
A ROLE = a set of expectations of how one will behave. Henry Mintzberg grouped 10 roles into 3 categories:

1. INTERPERSONAL — figurehead, leader, liaison
2. INFORMATIONAL — monitor, disseminator, spokesperson
3. DECISIONAL — entrepreneur, disturbance-handler, resource-allocator, negotiator
flashcards.explanation: Managers use interpersonal, informational and conceptual/decision-making skills as they play these roles.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE LEVELS of management (plus team leader & operatives)?
flashcards.answer:
1. TOP managers (CEO, president, VP) — manage the whole organization; set purpose, objectives, strategy.
2. MIDDLE managers (sales/branch manager, dept head) — implement top strategy via short-term operating plans.
3. FIRST-LINE managers (supervisor, crew leader) — implement operational plans; supervise OPERATIVE employees (not other managers).

+ TEAM LEADER (non-permanent, team-based) and NONMANAGEMENT OPERATIVE employees (do the actual work).
flashcards.explanation: Types by level: general managers, functional managers, project managers.

flashcards.question: CLASSICAL theory: who were Taylor, Fayol, Weber and Follett?
flashcards.answer:
Classical theorists focus on the JOB and management functions to find the best way to manage.

• Frederick TAYLOR — 'Father of Scientific Management' (job efficiency, time studies, wage incentives).
• Henri FAYOL — 'Father of Modern Management'; 5 functions + 14 principles (administrative theory).
• Max WEBER — developed the BUREAUCRACY concept (rules/procedures for fair treatment).
• Mary Parker FOLLETT — stressed PEOPLE; known for integrative conflict resolution.
flashcards.explanation: Scientific management = job efficiency; administrative theory = rules & organizational structure.

flashcards.question: BEHAVIORAL theory: who were Mayo, Maslow and McGregor?
flashcards.answer:
Behavioral theorists focus on PEOPLE (human skills over technical) to find the best way to manage.

• Elton MAYO — pioneered the HUMAN RELATIONS movement; how a manager treats people affects performance.
• Abraham MASLOW — hierarchy of needs theory (motivation).
• Douglas McGREGOR — Theory X (people dislike work, need control) vs Theory Y (people like to work, need little supervision).
flashcards.explanation: Behaviorists believed happy employees are productive — later research questioned this.

flashcards.question: What is the INTEGRATIVE perspective (systems, sociotechnical, contingency)?
flashcards.answer:
It integrates classical, behavioral and management-science theories. Three components:

1. SYSTEMS theory — view the organization as a WHOLE; an open system transforming inputs into outputs, interacting with the environment.
2. SOCIOTECHNICAL theory — integrate PEOPLE and TECHNOLOGY.
3. CONTINGENCY theory — there is no one best way; the best approach DEPENDS on the situation (stable→mechanistic, innovative→organic).
flashcards.explanation: Management science theorists use math (operations research, operations management, MIS) to aid decisions.

learn.title: Management & Its History
learn.content:
What is management?

Working with human, financial, physical and informational resources to achieve organizational objectives by performing four functions.

EFFICIENT = doing things RIGHT (least waste)  ·  EFFECTIVE = doing the RIGHT thing
PLANNING → ORGANIZING → LEADING → CONTROLLING (distinct yet interrelated)

Skills, roles & levels

  • Skills: technical (hard) · interpersonal (soft) · decision-making (conceptual)
  • Mintzberg's 10 roles → interpersonal · informational · decisional
  • Levels: top · middle · first-line (+ team leader, operatives)

Schools of management thought

  • Classical (the job): Taylor (scientific mgmt), Fayol (administrative), Weber (bureaucracy), Follett (people)
  • Behavioral (people): Mayo (human relations), Maslow (needs), McGregor (Theory X/Y)
  • Management science (math): operations research, MIS
  • Integrative: systems · sociotechnical · contingency ("it depends")

flashcards.question: What is the difference between PROBLEM SOLVING and DECISION MAKING?
flashcards.answer:
• A PROBLEM exists whenever objectives are not being met — a gap between what IS happening and what you WANT to happen.
• PROBLEM SOLVING = the process of taking corrective action to meet objectives.
• DECISION MAKING = the process of selecting a course of action that will solve a problem.
flashcards.explanation: Decision making is one of the three critical management skills.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE decision-making STYLES?
flashcards.answer:
1. REFLEXIVE — likes quick decisions ('shooting from the hip'), little information; decisive but can be wasteful.
2. REFLECTIVE — takes plenty of time, gathers much information; thorough but may procrastinate and lose opportunities.
3. CONSISTENT — neither rushes nor wastes time; knows when enough info is gathered → best record of good decisions.
flashcards.explanation: Reflexive too fast, reflective too slow, consistent = balanced.

flashcards.question: What are the 6 STEPS of the decision-making model?
flashcards.answer:
1. Classify and define the problem (or opportunity)
2. Set objectives and criteria
3. Generate creative & innovative alternatives
4. Analyze alternatives and select the most feasible
5. Plan and implement the decision
6. Control (monitor outcomes; take corrective action)
flashcards.explanation: Half of managers' decisions fail to solve the problems they target — following the model improves odds.

flashcards.question: PROGRAMMED vs NONPROGRAMMED decisions?
flashcards.answer:
• PROGRAMMED — recurring/routine situations; use decision rules, policies, procedures (e.g. reordering inventory). No need to follow all model steps.
• NONPROGRAMMED — significant, nonrecurring, nonroutine; expensive or major consequences (e.g. new product, new facility). Use the full decision-making model.
flashcards.explanation: Upper-level managers make more nonprogrammed decisions.

flashcards.question: What are the three DECISION-MAKING CONDITIONS?
flashcards.answer:
1. CERTAINTY — you know the outcome of each alternative in advance.
2. RISK — you don't know exact outcomes but can assign PROBABILITIES.
3. UNCERTAINTY — lack of information makes outcomes unpredictable; you cannot determine probabilities.
flashcards.explanation: High risk/uncertainty + significant decisions → use group decision making.

flashcards.question: MAXIMIZER vs SATISFICER?
flashcards.answer:
• MAXIMIZER — makes RATIONAL decisions; takes time, weighs a wide range of options to pick the BEST.
• SATISFICER (satisfy + suffice) — makes BOUNDED-rational decisions; fast over thorough; picks the first option meeting MINIMUM criteria.

Use maximizing for complex/nonprogrammed/high-risk decisions; satisficing for programmed/certain/low-importance ones.
flashcards.explanation: 'Must' criteria are essential; 'want' criteria are desirable and weighted by importance.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between CREATIVITY and INNOVATION?
flashcards.answer:
• CREATIVITY = a way of thinking that generates NEW ideas ('thinking outside the box'). It is the DRIVER of innovation.
• INNOVATION = the IMPLEMENTATION of a new idea.

Two types: PRODUCT innovation (new goods/services) and PROCESS innovation (new ways of doing things). Creativity is useless if not implemented.
flashcards.explanation: The 3 stages of the creative process: (1) preparation, (2) incubation & illumination, (3) evaluation.

flashcards.question: Name the 5 GROUP creativity techniques.
flashcards.answer:
1. BRAINSTORMING — suggesting many alternatives without evaluation (no criticism).
2. SYNECTICS — generating NOVEL alternatives via role-playing and fantasizing.
3. NOMINAL GROUPING — generate + evaluate via a structured voting method (6 steps).
4. CONSENSUS MAPPING — developing group AGREEMENT (Japanese 'ringi'); no vote forced.
5. DELPHI TECHNIQUE — series of confidential questionnaires to refine a solution (forecasting).
flashcards.explanation: Brainstorming/nominal/consensus = work groups; synectics/Delphi = upper-level managers.

flashcards.question: Name the main QUANTITATIVE decision techniques.
flashcards.answer:
• BREAK-EVEN analysis — sales volume at which there's no profit/loss.
• CAPITAL BUDGETING — analyze asset investments (payback, average rate of return, discounted cash flow).
• LINEAR PROGRAMMING — optimum allocation of scarce resources.
• QUEUING theory — balances the cost of waiting vs service capacity.
• PROBABILITY theory — assign probabilities, compute expected value (payoff matrix).
• BIG DATA — analysis of large quantified facts to maximize decisions.
flashcards.explanation: Quantitative = management science; uses math in the objective analysis of alternatives.

flashcards.question: What is OPPORTUNITY COST, and what is COST-BENEFIT analysis?
flashcards.answer:
• OPPORTUNITY COST = the next best alternative FOREGONE (e.g. €20 on a textbook means giving up the restaurant meal).
• COST-BENEFIT analysis = a MIXED technique comparing the cost vs benefit of each alternative using subjective judgment + some quantitative math (a mix of evidence-based management and judgment).
flashcards.explanation: Pros-and-cons analysis lists advantages (benefits) vs disadvantages (costs).

learn.title: Problem Solving & Decision Making
learn.content:
Core relationships

A problem = a gap between what is and what you want. Problem solving takes corrective action; decision making selects the action.

6-STEP MODEL: classify/define → set objectives & criteria → generate alternatives → analyze & select → plan/implement → control

Classifying the decision

  • Structure: programmed (routine, use rules) vs nonprogrammed (significant, use the model)
  • Conditions: certainty · risk (probabilities) · uncertainty
  • Type of maker: maximizer (rational, best) vs satisficer (bounded, "good enough")

Generating & analyzing alternatives

Creativity drives innovation (product & process). Group techniques: brainstorming · synectics · nominal grouping · consensus mapping · Delphi. Quantitative tools: break-even · capital budgeting · linear programming · queuing · probability · big data. Mixed: cost-benefit (+ opportunity cost, pros & cons, intuition).

flashcards.question: STRATEGIC vs OPERATIONAL planning?
flashcards.answer:
• STRATEGIC planning = developing a MISSION and LONG-RANGE objectives (usually 5 years, reviewed yearly) and how to accomplish them. Done by top/middle managers.
• OPERATIONAL planning = setting SHORT-RANGE objectives (one year or less) and how to meet them. Done by lower-level/functional managers.

Difference is mainly TIME FRAME and MANAGEMENT LEVEL.
flashcards.explanation: A strategy is a plan for pursuing a mission and achieving objectives.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 PLANNING LEVELS (corporate, business, functional)?
flashcards.answer:
• CORPORATE strategy — plan for managing MULTIPLE lines of business (strategic).
• BUSINESS strategy — plan for managing ONE line of business (strategic).
• FUNCTIONAL strategy — operational plan for managing ONE AREA of a business (marketing, operations, finance, HR).

Corporate + business = strategic planning; functional = operational planning.
flashcards.explanation: For a single-line firm, corporate and business strategies are the same.

flashcards.question: What are the 5 STEPS of the strategic planning PROCESS?
flashcards.answer:
1. Develop the MISSION (the foundation; based on a vision).
2. Analyze the ENVIRONMENT (situation analysis / SWOT).
3. Set OBJECTIVES.
4. Develop STRATEGIES (corporate, business, functional).
5. Implement and CONTROL strategies.

Not strictly linear — you may return to prior steps (an ongoing process).
flashcards.explanation: Mission is the foundation of the other four steps.

flashcards.question: What is a SWOT analysis and Porter's FIVE FORCES?
flashcards.answer:
• SWOT — internal STRENGTHS & WEAKNESSES (management, culture, resources, systems) + external OPPORTUNITIES & THREATS (customers, competitors, suppliers).
• Porter's FIVE FORCES — for industry/competitive analysis: rivalry among competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers.
flashcards.explanation: Part of step 2 (analyzing the environment / situation analysis).

flashcards.question: COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE, core competency and benchmarking?
flashcards.answer:
• COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE — specifies how a firm offers UNIQUE customer value ('what makes us different from and better than competitors?').
• CORE COMPETENCY — what a firm does WELL.
• BENCHMARKING — comparing your products/processes with those of OTHER companies (legally/ethically) to copy or improve them.
flashcards.explanation: Most benchmarking is within an industry, but non-competitors can inspire ideas too.

flashcards.question: What are the GRAND strategies?
flashcards.answer:
An overall corporate strategy:
1. GROWTH — aggressively increase size/sales.
2. STABILITY — hold present size or grow slowly (balance growth & profits).
3. TURNAROUND & RETRENCHMENT — turnaround reverses a declining business; retrenchment is divestiture/liquidation of assets (a SPINOFF sets up a unit as a separate company).
4. COMBINATION — a mix across different lines of business.
flashcards.explanation: SMART objectives = specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, timely.

flashcards.question: What are the three GROWTH strategies?
flashcards.answer:
1. CONCENTRATION — grow aggressively in the EXISTING line of business.
2. INTEGRATION — enter a related line: FORWARD (closer to the final customer, e.g. Apple Stores) or BACKWARD (farther from customer, e.g. Delta buying a refinery).
3. DIVERSIFICATION — go into RELATED (concentric) or UNRELATED (conglomerate) lines.

+ MERGERS & ACQUISITIONS (M&A): merger = two firms form one; acquisition = one buys another.
flashcards.explanation: Business portfolio analysis uses the BCG matrix to allocate resources among SBUs.

flashcards.question: What is the BCG GROWTH-SHARE MATRIX (4 cells)?
flashcards.answer:
Boston Consulting Group matrix for each business/product line:
• CASH COWS — generate more than they need; fund the others.
• STARS — question marks that succeeded (high growth, high share).
• QUESTION MARKS — entries into new businesses.
• DOGS — doing poorly; usually sold or liquidated.
flashcards.explanation: Used in corporate portfolio management (CPM) to allocate resources among strategic business units (SBUs).

flashcards.question: What are the ADAPTIVE and Porter's COMPETITIVE business-level strategies?
flashcards.answer:
ADAPTIVE (adapt to environmental change):
• PROSPECTING — aggressively offer new products/markets (≈ growth).
• DEFENDING — stay with present products/markets (≈ stability).
• ANALYZING — midrange between the two (≈ combination).

Porter's COMPETITIVE strategies:
• DIFFERENTIATION — stress distinctiveness (charge higher prices).
• COST LEADERSHIP — stress lower prices via tight cost control.
• FOCUS — target a specific niche/segment.
flashcards.explanation: Porter warns against mixing differentiation + cost leadership (you get 'stuck in the middle').

flashcards.question: STANDING vs SINGLE-USE vs CONTINGENCY plans?
flashcards.answer:
• STANDING plans — used repeatedly for routine issues: POLICIES (general guides), PROCEDURES/SOPs (sequence of actions), RULES (exactly what to do/not do).
• SINGLE-USE plans — for nonrepetitive situations: PROGRAMS and BUDGETS.
• CONTINGENCY plans — alternative 'backup' plans implemented if uncontrollable events occur.
flashcards.explanation: Most strategic plans are single-use; operational plans are more often standing plans.

learn.title: Strategic & Operational Planning
learn.content:
Two types, three levels

STRATEGIC (long-range, mission, top/middle)  vs  OPERATIONAL (≤1 year, functional)
LEVELS: corporate (many businesses) · business (one) · functional (one area)

The 5-step strategic planning process

  1. Develop the mission (foundation)
  2. Analyze the environment — SWOT + Porter's five forces
  3. Set objectives (SMART)
  4. Develop strategies (corporate / business / functional)
  5. Implement & control

Strategy menu

  • Grand: growth · stability · turnaround & retrenchment · combination
  • Growth: concentration · integration (forward/backward) · diversification (related/unrelated) · M&A
  • BCG: cash cows · stars · question marks · dogs
  • Adaptive: prospecting · defending · analyzing
  • Porter competitive: differentiation · cost leadership · focus
  • Plans: standing (policy/procedure/rule) · single-use (program/budget) · contingency

flashcards.question: What is ORGANIZING, and MECHANISTIC vs ORGANIC organizations?
flashcards.answer:
ORGANIZING (the 2nd management function) = the process of delegating and coordinating tasks and resources to achieve objectives.

• MECHANISTIC — bureaucratic: tight controls, rules/procedures, specialized jobs, top-down decisions. Works in STABLE environments.
• ORGANIC — flexible: minimal rules, broadly defined jobs, decisions at lower levels. Works in DYNAMIC environments.

They lie on a CONTINUUM.
flashcards.explanation: Larger firms tend to be more mechanistic; mass production → mechanistic; custom → organic.

flashcards.question: Name the key PRINCIPLES of organization.
flashcards.answer:
• UNITY OF COMMAND — each employee reports to ONLY ONE boss.
• UNITY OF DIRECTION — all activities directed toward the same objectives.
• CHAIN OF COMMAND (scalar principle) — clear line of authority top to bottom.
• SPAN OF MANAGEMENT (span of control) — number of employees reporting to a manager (tall = narrow spans; flat = wide spans).
• DIVISION OF LABOR — specialized jobs.
• COORDINATION — differentiation (split into departments) + integration (coordinate them).
flashcards.explanation: Mechanistic orgs enforce these principles more closely; flatter orgs cut management layers.

flashcards.question: RESPONSIBILITY, AUTHORITY, ACCOUNTABILITY and DELEGATION?
flashcards.answer:
• RESPONSIBILITY — obligation to achieve objectives by performing activities.
• AUTHORITY — the right to make decisions, issue orders, use resources.
• ACCOUNTABILITY — evaluation of how well one meets responsibilities.
• DELEGATION — assigning responsibility AND authority to accomplish objectives.

Responsibility & authority flow DOWN the chain of command; accountability flows UP. Delegation only occurs when you give a NEW task.
flashcards.explanation: You can be a manager without power, and have power without being a manager.

flashcards.question: AUTHORITY vs POWER; LINE vs STAFF; the 4 LEVELS of authority?
flashcards.answer:
• Authority = formal right from the organization; POWER = the ability to INFLUENCE others (broader).
• LINE authority — make decisions & issue orders down the chain (operations, marketing). STAFF authority — advise & assist (HR, PR, IT).
• 4 LEVELS of authority: (1) inform, (2) recommend, (3) report, (4) full authority.
flashcards.explanation: Formal authority = sanctioned; informal authority = unsanctioned (relationships).

flashcards.question: CENTRALIZED vs DECENTRALIZED authority?
flashcards.answer:
• CENTRALIZED — important decisions made by TOP managers. Advantages: control, reduced duplication. (Mechanistic.)
• DECENTRALIZED — important decisions made by MIDDLE and FIRST-LINE managers. Advantages: efficiency, flexibility. (Organic.)

MICROMANAGEMENT = a manager closely controls employees' work and avoids delegating — the opposite of empowerment.
flashcards.explanation: No single answer is best — it depends on the situation.

flashcards.question: What is DEPARTMENTALIZATION? Name the traditional types.
flashcards.answer:
Departmentalization = grouping related activities into units. Traditional types:
• FUNCTIONAL — by internal activity (production, sales, finance); used by small firms.
• PRODUCT (service) — by goods/services.
• CUSTOMER — by type of customer.
• TERRITORY (geographic) — by area (most MNCs).
• DIVISIONAL — semi-autonomous SBUs (M-form); CONGLOMERATE = unrelated profit centers.
• MATRIX — combines functional + product/divisional (employee has TWO bosses).
flashcards.explanation: Matrix's strength is flexibility; its weakness is violating unity of command (two bosses).

flashcards.question: Name the 5 CONTEMPORARY organizational designs.
flashcards.answer:
1. TEAM organization — based on teams (multiteam systems).
2. NETWORK organization — boundaryless interrelationships among firms (a hub + outside specialists).
3. MODULAR organization — design/market in-house, OUTSOURCE manufacturing (Nike, Dell).
4. VIRTUAL organization — evolving network of contingent workers/firms uniting temporarily (no central hub).
5. PLATFORM organization — connects buyers & sellers via the shared economy (Uber, Airbnb).
flashcards.explanation: REENGINEERING = fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes.

flashcards.question: What is JOB DESIGN — simplification vs expansion?
flashcards.answer:
JOB DESIGN = identifying the tasks each employee is responsible for.
• JOB SIMPLIFICATION — eliminate, combine, or change the sequence of tasks (more specialized; based on division of labor / Taylor). Work smarter, not harder.
• JOB EXPANSION — make jobs LESS specialized via:
  – ROTATION (perform different jobs in sequence; cross-training)
  – ENLARGEMENT (add tasks for variety)
  – ENRICHMENT (build MOTIVATORS into the job itself).
flashcards.explanation: Job enrichment uses flexible arrangements: telecommuting, flextime, compressed workweek, job sharing.

learn.title: Organizing & Delegating Work
learn.content:
Two ends of a continuum

MECHANISTIC (rules, tight control, specialized, top-down) ← → ORGANIC (flexible, broad jobs, lower-level decisions)
Stable environment → mechanistic  ·  Dynamic environment → organic

Principles & authority

  • Unity of command/direction · chain of command · span of management · division of labor · coordination
  • Responsibility & authority flow down; accountability flows up; delegation needs a NEW task
  • Authority vs power · line vs staff · centralized vs decentralized · 4 levels (inform/recommend/report/full)

Structure & jobs

  • Departmentalization: functional · product · customer · territory · divisional · matrix
  • Contemporary designs: team · network · modular · virtual · platform (+ reengineering)
  • Job design: simplification vs expansion (rotation · enlargement · enrichment)

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a GROUP and a TEAM?
flashcards.answer:
• GROUP — two or more members, a CLEAR leader, performing INDEPENDENT jobs with INDIVIDUAL accountability, evaluation and rewards.
• TEAM — a small number of members, SHARED leadership, performing INTERDEPENDENT jobs with INDIVIDUAL AND GROUP accountability, evaluation and rewards.

'All teams are groups, but not all groups are teams.'
flashcards.explanation: Continuum: management-directed (group) → semiautonomous → self-managed (team).

flashcards.question: What four factors make up the GROUP PERFORMANCE MODEL?
flashcards.answer:
Group performance = f(organizational context, group structure, group process, group development).

Groups/teams are the 'backbone' of organizations because of the SYSTEMS EFFECT — each group affects others and the total organization.
flashcards.explanation: Engaged teams grow profits about three times faster than disengaged ones.

flashcards.question: What are the dimensions of GROUP STRUCTURE?
flashcards.answer:
Group type, SIZE, COMPOSITION, leadership, and objectives.

Group TYPES: formal vs informal; functional (vertical) vs cross-functional (horizontal); command vs task (task force/ad hoc committee vs standing committee); plus GLOBAL VIRTUAL teams.
flashcards.explanation: Composition = the mix of members' skills and abilities; include diverse members.

flashcards.question: What is the ideal GROUP SIZE (and the 'two-pizza rule')?
flashcards.answer:
There is NO single ideal size, but generally 5–9 members give the best relationships and performance (short-term memory holds 7 ± 2 items).

• Too SMALL → limits ideas/creativity.
• Too LARGE → slow, less innovative, FREE-RIDING (social loafing).
• Amazon's TWO-PIZZA RULE: if two pizzas can't feed the team, it's too big (≤ ~8).
flashcards.explanation: Smaller groups < 5 risk groupthink; over 9, communication breaks down.

flashcards.question: What is GROUP PROCESS, and what are its dimensions?
flashcards.answer:
Group process (group dynamics) = the patterns of INTERACTIONS that emerge as members do their jobs (how they get along, not how they do the work).

Dimensions: ROLES, NORMS, COHESIVENESS, STATUS, decision making, and conflict resolution.
flashcards.explanation: The 3 group roles: task roles, maintenance roles, and self-interest roles.

flashcards.question: NORMS, COHESIVENESS and STATUS in a group?
flashcards.answer:
• NORMS — unwritten, shared expectations of appropriate behavior that develop as members interact (not set by management, unlike rules).
• COHESIVENESS — the extent to which members stick together; higher when goals are shared, the group is small/homogeneous, participation is equal, and it competes against external teams.
• STATUS — the perceived ranking of a member relative to others (based on performance, title, seniority, expertise, etc.).
flashcards.explanation: Groups listen more to high-status members and overlook their norm-breaking.

flashcards.question: What are TUCKMAN'S 5 stages of group development?
flashcards.answer:
Bruce Tuckman's stages:
1. FORMING (orientation) — low development; concerns about structure/leadership.
2. STORMING (dissatisfaction) — moderate development; frustration, conflict.
3. NORMING (resolution) — high development; members resolve differences.
4. PERFORMING (production) — outstanding development; works as a self-directed team.
5. TERMINATION (adjourning) — task groups disband.
flashcards.explanation: Two key variables: competence (rises over time) and commitment (starts high, drops, then rises).

flashcards.question: Which MANAGEMENT STYLE matches each development stage?
flashcards.answer:
• FORMING → AUTOCRATIC (high task, low support — tell them what to do).
• STORMING → CONSULTATIVE (high task, high support).
• NORMING → PARTICIPATIVE (low task, high support — share decisions).
• PERFORMING → EMPOWERMENT (low task, low support — let them decide; self-directed team).
• TERMINATION → no style needed.
flashcards.explanation: Change your leadership behavior as the group develops through the stages.

learn.title: Managing Teamwork
learn.content:
Group vs team

GROUP: clear leader · independent jobs · individual accountability
TEAM: shared leadership · interdependent jobs · individual + group accountability

Group performance model

performance = f(organizational context · structure · process · development). The systems effect links every group to the whole organization.

  • Structure: type · size (5–9 / two-pizza rule) · composition · leadership · objectives
  • Process: roles · norms · cohesiveness · status · decisions · conflict

Tuckman's stages → management style

  • Forming → autocratic
  • Storming → consultative
  • Norming → participative
  • Performing → empowerment (self-directed team)
  • Termination → no style needed

flashcards.question: What are the FOUR parts of the HRM (staffing) PROCESS?
flashcards.answer:
Human Resources Management = managing people for competitive advantage. Four parts:
1. PLANNING for human resources (strategic HR planning).
2. ATTRACTING employees (recruiting + selecting).
3. DEVELOPING employees (orientation, training, appraisal).
4. RETAINING employees (compensation, retention, separation).
flashcards.explanation: Also called the staffing process. HR is a STAFF department (advises/assists).

flashcards.question: What is JOB ANALYSIS (description vs specifications)?
flashcards.answer:
JOB ANALYSIS = determining what a position entails and the qualifications needed.
• JOB DESCRIPTION — identifies the TASKS and responsibilities of a position (often a Realistic Job Preview).
• JOB SPECIFICATIONS — identify the QUALIFICATIONS needed by the person to fill it.

Done BEFORE searching for a new employee.
flashcards.explanation: Making the job sound better than it is just creates turnover problems.

flashcards.question: What is RECRUITING, and the main internal/external sources?
flashcards.answer:
RECRUITING = attracting QUALIFIED candidates to apply (not just lots of applications).
• INTERNAL — promotions / lateral transfers ('internal mobility').
• EXTERNAL — employee REFERRALS (often the favorite; based on networking), walk-ins, outside organizations (schools/colleges/fairs), AGENCIES (temporary, public, private; executive 'headhunters'), advertising/internet/social media.
flashcards.explanation: More people get jobs through networking than all other methods combined.

flashcards.question: What are the 6 parts of the SELECTION PROCESS?
flashcards.answer:
1. APPLICATION form / résumé (used to screen)
2. SCREENING interviews (HR narrows the field)
3. TESTING
4. BACKGROUND & reference checks
5. INTERVIEWING (usually the MOST heavily weighted step)
6. HIRING

Not all parts are used for every job, and there's no fixed sequence.
flashcards.explanation: Selection = choosing the most qualified applicant while ensuring equal opportunity.

flashcards.question: In employment TESTING, what are VALIDITY and RELIABILITY?
flashcards.answer:
• VALIDITY — people who score HIGH on the test do WELL on the job (and low scorers do poorly). The test actually predicts job success.
• RELIABILITY — taking the same test on different days yields approximately the SAME score.

Large firms use ASSESSMENT CENTERS (tests + interviews + simulations).
flashcards.explanation: Tests include achievement, aptitude, personality, interest and physical exams.

flashcards.question: ORIENTATION/onboarding and TRAINING vs DEVELOPMENT?
flashcards.answer:
• ORIENTATION (now called ONBOARDING) — introducing new employees to the organization and their jobs; includes newcomer SOCIALIZATION (acquiring knowledge, skills, behaviors).
• TRAINING — teaching the skills necessary to perform the CURRENT job.
• DEVELOPMENT — ongoing education to improve skills for PRESENT and FUTURE jobs.
flashcards.explanation: Socialization is ranked more important than the formal orientation program.

flashcards.question: What is PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL and 360-degree feedback?
flashcards.answer:
PERFORMANCE APPRAISAL = the ongoing process of EVALUATING employee performance.

• Mechanistic orgs → manager evaluates subordinates.
• Organic self-managed teams → PEERS also evaluate each other (e.g. Zappos).
• 360-DEGREE feedback → evaluation expanded to everyone the employee contacts: peers, other departments, customers, suppliers.
flashcards.explanation: Used both for current performance and potential promotions.

flashcards.question: What is COMPENSATION — the 3 pay methods and benefits?
flashcards.answer:
COMPENSATION = total of pay + benefits (affects attracting AND retaining). PAY LEVEL = the choice to be a high-/medium-/low-paying firm.

Three PAY METHODS:
1. WAGES — paid hourly.
2. SALARY — based on time (week/month/year), regardless of hours.
3. INCENTIVES — pay for performance: piece rate, commissions, merit raises, bonuses, profit sharing, stock options.

BENEFITS = nonwage compensation (legally required: workers' comp, unemployment, Medicare, Social Security).
flashcards.explanation: The trend is pay for performance. Job evaluation determines each job's worth internally.

learn.title: Human Resource Management
learn.content:
The HRM (staffing) process

PLAN → ATTRACT (recruit + select) → DEVELOP (orient, train, appraise) → RETAIN (compensate)

Attracting

  • Job analysis → job description (tasks) + job specifications (qualifications)
  • Recruiting (qualified candidates): internal mobility · referrals · agencies · ads/social
  • Selection (6 steps): application → screening → testing (validity & reliability) → background → interview → hire

Developing & retaining

  • Onboarding + socialization; training (current job) vs development (future)
  • Performance appraisal (incl. 360-degree feedback)
  • Compensation = pay + benefits; methods: wages · salary · incentives
  • Labor unions & labor relations (collective bargaining)
